summary: Defines a way to compute a hash of a JSON Web Key. It specifies which fields are included, how to put them in a canonical form, and how to turn the result into bytes to hash. The hash can be used to identify or select a key.

plainLanguage.summary: A digital key can be written down in many slightly different ways, and it may carry extra notes about itself. This document gives a fixed recipe for turning a key into one short fingerprint, so two copies of the same key always give the same answer.

subtitle: A recipe for turning a JSON Web Key into a short, repeatable hash that names the key.

tldr.problem: A JSON Web Key can be written in many ways and can carry extra optional members, so there was no agreed way to compute a hash that identifies the key itself.
tldr.mechanism: Keep only the required members of the key, write them as JSON with no whitespace and in lexicographic order, then hash the UTF-8 octets with a chosen hash function such as SHA-256.
tldr.outcome: The same key gives the same thumbprint no matter which optional members travel with it, so the base64url-encoded thumbprint can serve as a key ID.

facts.label: Hash input
facts.value: UTF-8 octets of the canonical JSON object

today: RFC 7638 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2015, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the JSON Web Key specification, RFC 7517.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: The specification defines a method for computing a hash value, also called a digest, over a JSON Web Key. It defines which fields in a JWK are used in the hash computation, the method of creating a canonical form for those fields, and how to convert the resulting Unicode string into a byte sequence to be hashed. The resulting hash value can be used for identifying or selecting the key represented by the JWK that is the subject of the thumbprint, for instance by using the base64url-encoded JWK Thumbprint value as a 'kid', or key ID, value.
sections.plainLanguage: The document defines one fixed way to turn a key into a short fingerprint, so that the same key always produces the same fingerprint however it was written down.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content: The specification uses the same terminology as the JSON Web Key, JSON Web Signature and JSON Web Algorithms specifications. It defines one term of its own: the JWK Thumbprint is the digest value for a JWK.
sections.plainLanguage: A JWK Thumbprint is simply the fingerprint of a key. Nothing else in the document uses a new term.

sections.title: Computing the JWK Thumbprint
sections.content:
The thumbprint of a JSON Web Key is computed in two steps.

First, construct a JSON object containing only the required members of a JWK representing the key, with no whitespace or line breaks before or after any syntactic elements, and with the required members ordered lexicographically by the Unicode code points of the member names. That JSON object is itself a legal JWK representation of the key.

Second, hash the octets of the UTF-8 representation of that JSON object with a cryptographic hash function H. SHA-256 might be used as H. The resulting value is the JWK Thumbprint with H of the JWK.

Section 3.4 discusses the choice of hash function. A specific hash function must be chosen by an application. While SHA-256 is a good default choice at the time of writing, the hash function of choice can be expected to change over time as the cryptographic landscape evolves. In many cases only the party that creates a key needs to know the hash function used: a typical usage is for the producer of the key to use the base64url-encoded JWK Thumbprint value as a 'kid' value, and the consumer of the 'kid' treats it as an opaque value it uses to select the key. In other cases multiple parties reproduce the calculation and compare the results, and then they need to know which hash function was used and use the same one.

A key need not be in JWK format to create a JWK Thumbprint of it. The only prerequisites are that the JWK representation of the key is defined and that the party creating the thumbprint is in possession of the necessary key material.
sections.plainLanguage: Two steps: write the key down in a fixed, tidy way, then hash the bytes of that text. The hash function is a choice the application makes, usually SHA-256.

sections.title: Example Thumbprint Computation
sections.content:
The document works through an RSA key that carries four members: 'kty' set to RSA, the modulus 'n', the exponent 'e' set to AQAB, and two optional members, 'alg' set to RS256 and 'kid' set to 2011-04-29. The required members for an RSA public key are 'kty', 'n' and 'e', so those three are the ones used in the thumbprint computation.

In lexicographic order the members are 'e', 'kty' and 'n'. The intermediate JSON object is therefore the three members written with no spaces, in that order, with the modulus as one long string. The octets of its UTF-8 representation are then hashed with SHA-256 as the hash function H, which gives the JWK SHA-256 Thumbprint value. Its base64url encoding, which might for instance be used as a 'kid' value, is NzbLsXh8uDCcd-6MNwXF4W_7noWXFZAfHkxZsRGC9Xs.
sections.plainLanguage: The worked example takes an RSA key with five members, keeps only the three the key type requires, writes them in alphabetical order with no spaces, and hashes the result.

sections.title: JWK Members Used in the Thumbprint
sections.content:
Only the required members of a key's representation are used when computing its thumbprint. For an elliptic curve public key, for the curves specified in Section 6.2.1.1 of RFC 7518, the required members in lexicographic order are 'crv', 'kty', 'x' and 'y'. For an RSA public key they are 'e', 'kty' and 'n'. For a symmetric key they are 'k' and 'kty'. As other 'kty' key type values are defined, the specifications defining them should be consulted to determine which members, in addition to 'kty', are required.

The thumbprint of a JWK representing a private key is computed as the thumbprint of a JWK representing the corresponding public key. This has the intentional benefit that the same thumbprint value can be computed both by parties using either the public or the private key, so the thumbprint can refer to both keys of the pair. Application context can then be used to determine whether the public or the private key is the one being referred to. The specification defines the method for private keys for interoperability reasons, so that different implementations computing thumbprints of private keys produce the same result.

Optional members of JWKs are intentionally left out, so that their absence or presence does not alter the resulting value. The thumbprint is a digest of the members required to represent the key as a JWK, not of additional data that may also accompany the key. Optional members are left out so that the thumbprint refers to a key, not to a key with an associated set of key attributes: different application contexts might include different subsets of optional attributes, and if those were included the values would differ for JWKs even though the keys are the same. Other specifications could define different kinds of thumbprint that include some or all of the additional members, if use cases arise where those would be useful.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the fields that make up the key itself go into the fingerprint. Notes such as the algorithm or a key identifier are left out, so the fingerprint stays the same however the key is annotated.

sections.title: Order and Representation of Members
sections.content:
The required members in the input to the hash function are ordered lexicographically by the Unicode code points of the member names.

Characters in member names and member values MUST be represented without being escaped. This means that thumbprints of JWKs that require such characters are not defined by this specification, though in practice the members of JWK representations are not expected to use any of these characters. The characters specified as requiring escaping by Section 7 of RFC 7159 are the quotation mark, the reverse solidus or backslash, and the control characters U+0000 through U+001F.

If the JWK key type uses members whose values are themselves JSON objects, the members of those objects MUST likewise be lexicographically ordered. If the key type uses members whose values are JSON numbers, and those numbers are integers, they MUST be represented as a JSON number without a fraction part or an exponent part, so for instance the value '1.024e3' MUST be represented as '1024'. This means that thumbprints of JWKs using numbers that are not integers are not defined by this specification. As noted in the I-JSON Message Format specification, implementations cannot expect an integer whose absolute value is greater than 9007199254740991, that is, outside the safe integer range, to be treated as an exact value.
sections.plainLanguage: The fields are sorted by the code points of their names, and the text is written plainly with no escape sequences and no spaces. Anything that needs escaping is outside what the document defines.

sections.title: Practical JSON and Unicode Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations will almost certainly use functionality provided by the platform's JSON support when parsing the JWK and emitting the JSON object used as the hash input. As a practical consideration, future JWK member names and values should be avoided for which different platforms or libraries might emit different representations. As of the time of writing, all defined JWK member names and values use only printable ASCII characters, which should not exhibit this problem. However, JSON.stringify() cannot be counted on to lexicographically sort the members of JSON objects, so while it could be used to emit some kinds of member values, different code is likely to be needed to perform the sorting.

While the operation of lexicographically ordering member names by their Unicode code points is well defined, different platform sort functions may produce different results for non-ASCII characters, in ways that may not be obvious to developers. If writers of future specifications defining new JWK key type values restrict themselves to printable ASCII member names and values, some future interoperability problems might be avoided. If new JWK members are defined that use non-ASCII member names or values, their definitions should specify the exact Unicode code point sequences used to represent them, which is particularly important where Unicode normalization could transform one set of code points into another.

Use of escaped characters in JWKs for which JWK Thumbprints will be computed should be avoided, and use of escaped characters in the hash input JWKs derived from these original JWKs is prohibited. Number representations containing fraction or exponent parts in JWKs for which thumbprints will be computed should also be avoided. All of these practical considerations are an instance of Jon Postel's principle: be liberal in what you accept, and conservative in what you send.

JWK Thumbprint values are computed on the JWK members required to represent a key, rather than on all the members of the JWK the key is represented in. They are therefore more analogous to applications that use digests of X.509 Subject Public Key Info values than to applications that use digests of complete certificate values, as the 'x5t' value defined for X.509 certificate objects does. While logically equivalent to a digest of the Subject Public Key Info representation of the key, a JWK Thumbprint is computed over a JSON representation of that key rather than over an ASN.1 representation of it.
sections.plainLanguage: Different JSON libraries may write the same data in slightly different ways, so the document asks key types to stick to plain ASCII characters and warns that the built-in sorting function in most languages cannot be relied on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The JSON Security Considerations and Unicode Comparison Security Considerations described in Sections 10.12 and 10.13 of the JSON Web Signature specification also apply.

Some implementations may produce incorrect results if esoteric or escaped characters are used in member names. The security implications of this appear to be limited for thumbprints of public keys, because while it may result in implementations failing to identify the intended key, it should not leak information: the information in a public key is already public by definition.

A hash of a symmetric key has the potential to leak information about the key value. The thumbprint of a symmetric key should therefore typically be concealed from parties not in possession of the symmetric key, unless the application context is one where the cryptographic hash used, such as SHA-256, is known to provide sufficient protection against disclosure of the key value.

A JWK Thumbprint will only uniquely identify a particular key if a single unambiguous JWK representation for that key is defined and used when computing it. For example, if an RSA key used 'e' as 'AAEAAQ', representing the bytes [0, 1, 0, 1], rather than the correct representation 'AQAB', representing [1, 0, 1], then a different thumbprint value would be produced for what could be effectively the same key, at least for implementations that are lax in validating the JWK values they accept. Thumbprint values can therefore only be relied upon to be unique for a given key if the implementation also validates that the correct representation of the key is used.

Even more insidious is that an attacker may supply a key that is a transformation of a legal key in order to have it appear to be a different key. If a legitimate RSA key uses a modulus value N and an attacker supplies a key with modulus 3*N, the modified key would still work about a third of the time but would appear to be a different key. Thumbprint values are therefore valuable for identifying legitimate keys, but comparing thumbprint values is not a reliable means of excluding, or blacklisting, the use of particular keys or transformations of them.
sections.plainLanguage: The fingerprint of a public key is harmless to publish. The fingerprint of a shared secret may leak the secret, so keep it private. And a fingerprint only identifies a key if both sides use the standard form of that key.

viz.caption: THE TWO STEPS OF THE COMPUTATION (RFC 7638, SECTION 3)

items.title: Write the canonical JSON
items.text: Keep only the required members, order them lexicographically by the Unicode code points of their names, and write them with no whitespace or line breaks.

items.title: Hash the UTF-8 bytes
items.text: Take the octets of the UTF-8 representation of that JSON object and hash them with the chosen cryptographic hash function H, for example SHA-256.

items.title: Encode the result
items.text: The base64url encoding of the digest is the value to publish, and it can be used as a key ID.
